source.title: Sparsity and Superposition in Mixture of Experts
source.authors: Marmik Chaudhari; Jeremi Nuer; Rome Thorstenson

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendix, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures superposition in toy networks and compares dense and MoE representations, using a toy-model extension of earlier superposition work.
record.gate_note: The study tests synthetic toy autoencoders, not real vision neurons or transformer language-model neurons. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows. Individual cells in the phase-diagram figures are not separately extracted where the text does not describe their outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study trains toy autoencoders in the Elhage et al. superposition framework, a new setting for V3's mechanism. Its dense models pack more sparse features than dimensions, and routing reduces superposition. It measures superposition (features per dimension, interference), not neuron polysemanticity; the authors say less superposition is not basis-aligned monosemantic neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MoEs show less superposition than dense models and no sharp phase changes, and that network sparsity better characterizes them. They add a feature-based definition of expert specialization: experts organize around coherent features when initialized appropriately. They note that 'monosemantic' here means less superposition, not basis-aligned neurons, and that transfer to large transformers is uncertain.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts the toy superposition framework to mixture-of-experts models and measures feature interference and representation properties in synthetic autoencoders; it does not reproduce the original vision-neuron example.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature sparsity, relative feature importance, expert count/network sparsity, and model setup (n and m) change the representation outcomes. The authors also describe a mixed region around 0.48–0.7 feature sparsity in some setups.

fits_no_version.finding: MoE toy models with more experts at equal total parameters have fewer features per dimension (less superposition) than dense models. The cost is ~0.03–0.08 higher reconstruction loss, which narrows as expert count grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture (MoE routing / network sparsity) reduces superposition in toy models at a small reconstruction-loss cost. This is a superposition analogue of V5, not a measured share of polysemantic neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: MoE experts lack the dense models' discrete phase changes. Transitions are more continuous, with a mixed region at ~0.48–0.7 feature sparsity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Network sparsity, rather than feature sparsity and importance alone, governs superposition phase behaviour in toy MoEs.

record.problems: All experiments use simple toy autoencoders with synthetic independent features, not realistic data or large language models. The authors note restricted routing and architecture choices and say transfer to real-world MoEs is uncertain. Some results are described qualitatively from plots without exact cell values. Reconstruction loss is measured, but downstream performance and training stability at scale are not evaluated.
record.rows_left_out: Individual expert/cell results from Figures 4 and 5 and exact plotted values from Figures 3 and 6 are not separately transcribed where the text does not provide their values; the relevant textual aggregate findings are recorded in the rows.

untested.parts: Real trained networks (vision or language); neuron-level polysemanticity, as opposed to superposition measured as features per dimension; non-synthetic, correlated features.

missing.what: Expert specialization results. Router initialization (diagonal, ordered k-hot, random k-hot) determines which features experts represent monosemantically. Usage statistics over 1000 experts are in Table 1, e.g. 461/1000 Xavier experts have 0 monosemantic features. Not recorded or declared in rows_left_out.
missing.versions: none (initialization effect under capacity pressure; not V4)

missing.what: A small dense model (n=20, m=6) represents 10 features, against 8 for a 3-expert MoE. The MoE has block-diagonal interference.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. V5 is not credited because the study measures superposition, not the share of polysemantic neurons, and explicitly separates the two. The loss rows matter only to the fits_no_version entry. V1, V2, V4, V6 and V7 are not tested. Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is a new MoE toy setting, not the original methods.

versions.untested_parts: Vision classifiers and individual neurons such as InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55.
Transformer language models, MLP neurons, tokens or contexts.
The experiments use synthetic features and toy autoencoders; they do not establish that superposition is the cause of polysemanticity in trained large-scale networks.
The study does not test polysemanticity without capacity pressure. Its initialization comparisons do not establish that there is enough capacity for every feature.
It tests dense versus MoE architecture and expert count in toy models, not SoLU, modern convnets, or regularization changes. It does not evaluate large-scale downstream performance.
The study does not reassess canonical polysemantic neurons or test whether their mixed inputs share a feature.
The study does not vary activation-range selection or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: MoE setup A (n=2, m=1)
rows.size_stated: n=2; m=1 per expert; E varied
rows.operation_detail: Measured the last feature's norm and superposition over feature sparsity and relative importance.
rows.measure: Last-feature representation and superposition phase diagrams.
rows.value: With increased expert count, discrete phase changes disappeared and transitions were more continuous; the MoE preserved the last feature more than the dense model when feature sparsity was low.
rows.note: The authors describe these qualitative outcomes; exact cell values are in the figure.
rows.check: Phase-diagram continuity in MoE experts is a representation-strategy result. It does not show whether neurons are polysemantic or why.

rows.subject: MoE setup B (n=3, m=1)
rows.size_stated: n=3; m=1 per expert; E varied
rows.operation_detail: Measured the last feature's norm and superposition over feature sparsity and relative importance.
rows.measure: Last-feature representation and superposition phase diagrams.
rows.value: MoEs generally did not show a clear phase change, but the region around 0.5–0.7 feature sparsity in B.2/2 was mostly discrete and mixed. In this setup, experts could superimpose the other two features, leaving no space for the third in one hidden dimension.
rows.note: The authors explicitly identify this as an exception to the general absence of clear MoE phase changes.
rows.check: Same as r6. The 'partial' state was set against no version.

relationships.condition: Toy ReLU autoencoders with synthetic sparse features (dense n=100,m=20; dense n=2–3,m=1–2)
relationships.reason: The dense model packs more features than dimensions, and this rises with feature sparsity with a clear phase change (r1, r5). Routing that cuts per-expert interference lowers features per dimension, consistent with a capacity-pressure cause (r2–r4).
relationships.display_finding: The dense model represented more features than dimensions, and this rose with feature sparsity through a clear phase change. Expert routing that cut per-expert interference lowered features per dimension, consistent with capacity pressure as the cause.

tranche.reason: New setting (toy MoE autoencoders) with results that bear on superposition. Its dense phase diagrams are a comparator replication of Elhage et al., so T3 fits.

source_check.notes: Features per dimension and the superposition score measure feature superposition, not neuron polysemanticity; the authors say so in Section 3. Exact values are given only in figures. The phase-diagram section (Section 5) fixes active parameters, while Section 4.2 fixes total parameters. The l0 condition names only the dense models, but its reason also uses the MoE rows r2-r4. The paper contradicts itself on whether Section 4 uses load balancing.
